passages.t: Flee from Jerusalem: the siege ramp is raised
passages.happening:
“Run for cover, O sons of Benjamin; flee from Jerusalem!” (verse 1). The ram's horn sounds in Tekoa and a signal goes up over Beth-haccherem, for disaster looms from the north. God will destroy the Daughter of Zion, beautiful and delicate as she is (verse 2).

Shepherds and their flocks come against her and pitch their tents all around (verse 3). The soldiers urge one another to attack at noon, then complain that the daylight is fading, and decide to attack by night (verses 4 and 5).

‘Cut down the trees and raise a siege ramp against Jerusalem’ (verse 6). The city must be punished, for there is nothing but oppression in her. ‘As a well gushes its water, so she pours out her evil’ (verse 7). Violence and destruction echo in her streets. Jerusalem must take warning, or God will turn away and make her a desolation (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The places are precise. Benjamin, Jeremiah's own tribe, lay just north of Jerusalem. Its people had fled into the capital for safety, and now they are told to flee out of it. Tekoa was a town south of Jerusalem, the home of Amos. The alarm sounds on every side.

Ancient armies besieged walled cities by cutting trees to build ramps of earth and timber up to the walls, so that battering rams could reach the gates. Deuteronomy forbade Israel to cut down fruit trees for siegeworks, but invaders had no such scruple.

The shepherds with their flocks are the enemy kings and their armies, each taking a share of the land like a pasture. The soldiers' eagerness, attacking at noon, then by night, adds to the terror.

The chapter, like chapters 4 and 5, is undated poetry. It is usually placed in the years when Babylon's threat was taking shape, though it describes a siege like the one that came in 588 to 586 BC.
passages.later: The law said that in a siege, ‘you must not destroy its trees’ that bear fruit (Deuteronomy 20:19). Amos, the shepherd from Tekoa, had brought the same charge of oppression against the north (Amos 3:9).
passages.asks: God says Jerusalem pours out evil as a well pours out water. Ask what flows out of your life without your noticing. And ask whether you can still take warning before it is too late.

passages.t: Peace, peace, when there is no peace
passages.happening:
God says the remnant of Israel will be gleaned like a vine (verse 9). Jeremiah answers: whom can he warn? Their ears are closed, and the word of the LORD has become offensive to them (verse 10). He is full of God's wrath and tired of holding it in (verse 11). Houses, fields and wives will be handed to others (verse 12).

‘For from the least of them to the greatest, all are greedy for gain; from prophet to priest, all practice deceit’ (verse 13). They dress the people's wound with very little care and say all is peace, ‘when there is no peace at all’ (verse 14). They do not even know how to blush (verse 15).

‘Stand at the crossroads and look. Ask for the ancient paths’ (verse 16). Walk in the good way, ‘and you will find rest for your souls’ (verse 16). But they refuse, and they will not listen to the watchmen's horn (verse 17). What use to God is frankincense from Sheba or sweet cane from far away? Their sacrifices do not please him (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The false prophets treated a deep wound as a scratch. They told the people all was well, because that is what the people wanted to hear, and they did not call anyone to change. Jeremiah says their healing is no healing at all.

The crossroads was a place where travelers had to choose. The ancient paths are the old ways of the covenant, the good way the fathers had been shown. The people are told to ask for them and walk in them. They refuse.

Sheba was a kingdom in southern Arabia, famous for frankincense, carried north by caravan along the incense routes. Costly offerings brought from far away mean nothing to God from people who will not listen to him.
passages.later: Ezekiel brings the same charge against false prophets who say ‘Peace,’ when there is no peace (Ezekiel 13:10). Jesus takes up the words of verse 16: ‘you will find rest for your souls’ (Matthew 11:29).
passages.hard:
How can anyone tell a true word of peace from the false peace Jeremiah condemns?

The prophets Jeremiah opposed spoke in God's name and promised safety. On the surface their message sounded more like good news than his, and many sincere people believed them. The book gives several tests. Their words did not deal with sin: they healed the wound lightly, reassuring people without calling them to change (verse 14; 23:17). Their lives did not match their message, for all of them, prophet and priest, were greedy for gain (verse 13). And in the end, a word is shown to be true when it comes to pass.

A true word of peace does not deny the wound. It names it, and it points to the good way.
passages.asks: The people were offered rest for their souls and refused to walk in it. Ask whether there is an old, good way you have refused because it asked something of you. And ask whose comfort you trust because it never asks you to change.

passages.t: A cruel army, and rejected silver
passages.happening:
‘Behold, an army is coming from the land of the north’ (verse 22). They grasp bow and spear and are cruel and merciless. ‘Their voice roars like the sea’ (verse 23). The people's hands hang limp, and pain grips them like a woman in labor (verse 24). They must not go out to the fields or walk the road, for terror is on every side (verse 25).

‘O daughter of my people, dress yourselves in sackcloth and roll in ashes’ (verse 26). They are to mourn as for an only son.

God tells Jeremiah he has appointed him to test the people like ore (verse 27). They are hardened rebels and slanderers, bronze and iron (verse 28). ‘The bellows blow fiercely, blasting away the lead with fire. The refining proceeds in vain, for the wicked are not purged’ (verse 29). ‘They are called rejected silver, because the LORD has rejected them’ (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Mourning for an only son was the deepest grief the first hearers knew. It meant the end of a family's future.

The last verses draw on metalwork. Silver was refined by heating the ore with lead in a furnace while bellows blew air across it. The lead carried off the impurities and left pure silver. Jeremiah is set to test the people like ore. But the lead burns away and the dross stays. The refining fails, and the silver is thrown out.

Terror on every side, magor missabib, becomes a phrase Jeremiah repeats, and in chapter 20 it becomes his nickname for the priest who beat him.
passages.later: Ezekiel uses the same picture of Israel as metal in a furnace: ‘They are but the dross of silver’ (Ezekiel 22:18). And Jeremiah later renames the priest who beat him ‘Magor-missabib’ (Jeremiah 20:3), terror on every side.
passages.asks: The refining did not work because the people would not let go of their dross. Ask what God may be trying to burn away in you, and whether you are holding on to it. And ask what it would mean to mourn over sin as you would over a great loss.
